topic.title: We read 1-star reviews to buy
topic.claim: We read 1-star reviews to decide to buy, not to avoid. If the complaint is about delivery, we're sold.
topic.moment: You skip the 5 stars and go straight to the angriest review, which says 'box came dented'.

turn.actually: Bad reviews are the only ones we trust, so a harmless complaint works as an endorsement.

topic.feeling: Relieved I finally have a reason to trust something.
topic.villain: Review sections so full of paid praise that only complaints feel real
topic.because: We know 5-star reviews can be bought. A real complaint about a small thing proves the product survived real use.
topic.payoff: The best review a brand can get is a 1-star about the courier.
topic.behaviour: Shoppers filter by lowest rating first and buy if the flaws are irrelevant to them.
topic.mechanism: Paid praise made complaints the only signal left.
topic.group: Online shoppers who research before buying
topic.send_to: The friend who takes 40 minutes to buy a kettle
topic.why_now: Paid and fake reviews have made star ratings feel useless.

score.why: We go straight to the angriest review, and a harmless complaint ends up working as an endorsement. It's a funny, true habit most people never examine.

notes: slide 6: This slide works against the post. It says negative reviews get ignored, which means the 1-stars we trust are also filtered. That undercuts 'only honest signal' and the slide 7 line 'it still isn't overthinking' doesn't answer it. Either turn it into a twist (the source says 27% saw their reviews published unchanged, so the angry ones that survive feel even more real) or cut the filtering line and keep only 'half check reviews before every purchase', stated plainly as support. Right now it reads like a fact dump in the middle of an opinion post.

slide 5: 'has told you everything. He used the product.' overclaims. A complaint about the box doesn't prove the buyer used the product. Say it straight but smaller: if the courier is the worst thing he could find, the product gave him nothing to complain about. Also cut 'He was hunting for a problem', which is a guess.

slides 4, 5 and 7: The idea 'paid 5-stars, so complaints are the only honest reviews' is said three times (the cashback card, 'only reviews nobody paid for', 'when every star can be bought'). Merge them. Let slide 4 carry the cause, slide 5 carry the courier-complaint logic, and make slide 7 add something new, such as what the shopper actually feels when they find the dented-box review (relief, finally something to trust).

slide 3: This is the funniest slide, but the examples switch products (mixer, kettle) and the 'best review on the page' line is the only real turn. Pick one product so the reader sees a single scroll through the angry reviews. Add one sensory or insider detail, for example scrolling past the all-caps rants and stopping at the polite one.

slide 8: 'It doesn't even mention the product' repeats what the line before it already shows. Let 'The best review a brand can get is a 1-star about the courier.' stand alone as the closer, or swap the second line for a sting, such as the brand never realising which review is doing its selling.

violations: Dead slide (7): slide 6, 'In a LocalCircles survey of over 33,000 Indians, half said they check reviews before every online purchase. So this isn't a quirk of the kettle friend.' The stat only says people check reviews. It says nothing about sorting by lowest rating or buying because of a complaint, so it can't back the claim, and the line 'isn't a quirk of the kettle friend' overreaches. It also slows the turn that slide 5 had just landed. 'Here's the funny part' is stock scaffolding.

Decorative invented specifics / dangling reference: slide 6 'the kettle friend' and slide 7 'Forty minutes for a kettle' refer to a friend and a duration the post body never introduces (they come only from the send line, which readers of these cards don't see).
notes: slide 6: Cut or replace. The sourced fact that actually fits the thesis is that the same survey found negative reviews often go unpublished. Use it, stated plainly: even the angry reviews you find are the ones the platform let through, so a harmless 1-star is more believable. Drop 'Here's the funny part' and the 'kettle friend' line. Do not stretch the 50% stat to mean people read 1-stars first.

slide 7: Remove 'Forty minutes for a kettle'. Either set up the long hunt in slide 2 ('twenty tabs open for a kettle') or end on the relief line: 'finally a stranger with nothing to sell'. The slide is also a bit too tidy and explains a feeling the reader already had. Trust the image and trim.

slide 3: The third bullet, 'Returned it, changed my mind', is not a complaint about a harmless thing. It is a return, which reads as a mild warning, and calling it the 'best review on the page' blurs the rule. Swap it for another harmless gripe, such as 'Packaging had too much plastic', so all three bullets prove the same point. Add one detail beyond sight, such as the rattle of the lid or the heft of the box.

slide 5: Good logic, but state the rule from the inside more sharply, e.g. a complaint about the courier is a review of someone else's job. Also introduce the kettle in slide 2 ('You're buying a kettle') so slide 3 doesn't arrive cold.

slide 8: Keep the courier line. The brand-reply beat is a good sting, but make it more concrete: the brand pastes the same apology under a courier rant and a real defect, so it can't tell which 1-star is its gift.

sources.fact: A LocalCircles survey of over 33,000 Indians found half check ratings and reviews before every online purchase and 35% do so sometimes. It also found that negative reviews often go unpublished, so shoppers may see fewer 1-star reviews than exist. The survey does not measure sorting by lowest rating or buying because a complaint is irrelevant, so the claim's specific behaviour is unverified.
sources.excerpt: 50% of the respondents said they do check the ratings and reviews of the product before proceeding to buy. [...] their negative reviews on products were either ignored [...] 27% said their reviews were published unchanged. [...] survey of "over 33,000 people" from "more than 220 districts across India."

cover.headline: We read [1-star reviews] to buy, not to avoid
cover.sub: The angrier the review, the faster we tap Add to Cart.

paragraphs: We don't read 1-star reviews to avoid a product. We read them to buy it.
slides.why_swipe: How does a bad review make anyone buy?

paragraphs: You're buying a kettle, with twenty tabs open. You skip the 4.5 stars and the two thousand "Excellent product!!" reviews. You tap the filter. Lowest rating first.
And there it is, in angry capitals: "BOX CAME DENTED. VERY BAD SERVICE."
The next one says "Box too heavy to carry upstairs." That's a solid kettle.
slides.why_swipe: Why do we trust the angry ones over the happy ones?

paragraphs: Plenty of 5-stars come from a card in the box: "Rate us 5 stars, get ₹100 cashback."
So they all sound the same. "Nice product, value for money."
Once you've seen that card, every 5-star looks like someone who took the ₹100.
Look at who the angry buyer is actually angry with.
A complaint about the courier is a review of someone else's job.
If a dented box is the worst thing an angry buyer could find, the kettle gave him nothing to complain about.
slides.why_swipe: But are the angry reviews even all there?

paragraphs: And the angry ones are rarer than they should be. A LocalCircles survey of over 33,000 Indians found negative reviews often never get published.
So a 1-star you can still see feels like it slipped through.
slides.why_swipe: So what do we feel when we finally find one?

paragraphs: What you feel when you find the dented-box review isn't suspicion. It's relief.
Finally, a stranger with nothing to sell.
slides.why_swipe: So what's the review every brand should actually want?

paragraphs: The best review a brand can get is a 1-star about the courier.
slides.why_swipe: Does the brand even know which 1-star helped it?

paragraphs: Same "We're sorry for the inconvenience" under the courier rant and under the kettle that actually leaked.
The brand can't tell which 1-star was the gift.

end.save: Open it again the next time you sort by lowest rating first.
end.send: Send to the friend who takes 40 minutes to buy a kettle and still reads the angry reviews twice.

draft.caption: What's the most useless 1-star review that made you buy something anyway?
draft.alt_text: A nine-slide text post arguing that Indian online shoppers read 1-star reviews to decide to buy. Shoppers skip the 5-star reviews, many of which follow a cashback card in the box and all sound the same, and sort by lowest rating. A complaint about a dented box or the courier is a review of someone else's job, so the product gave the buyer nothing to complain about. A LocalCircles survey found negative reviews often go unpublished, so a harmless 1-star that is still visible feels like proof. It closes: the best review a brand can get is a 1-star about the courier, and the brand pastes the same apology under it as under a kettle that actually leaked, unable to tell which 1-star was the gift.

claims.text: A LocalCircles survey of over 33,000 Indians found negative reviews often never get published.
